title: Baby Dolls
strapline: Shh — the baby's sleeping. Feeding, bathing, rocking: the tenderest work in the room.
intent: Caring for a baby lets children practise the nurture they receive — feeding, bathing, dressing, soothing — and pass it on.
The baby's needs give feelings a safe distance: children name the baby's crying, tiredness and hunger, and work out what will help.
Doll care is genuinely fiddly work — poppers, spoon-feeding, wrapping a swaddle, fastening the pram straps — small hands doing real jobs.
Looking after 'my baby' invites children to talk about their own babyhood and their own families — who cared for them, and how.
Lullabies, nappy-change chatter and the running narration of a baby's day keep language flowing quietly and constantly.
For children with a new sibling at home, this is where the biggest change in their life gets worked through.
implementation: Treat the dolls as babies, always — carried carefully, spoken to softly, never left face-down on the floor — and children will follow.
Model parentese and care talk: 'You're crying, little one — are you hungry, or do you need a sleep? Let's try a feed first.'
Wonder aloud about the baby's feelings and let children do the deciding: 'Why do you think she's still crying? What else could we try?'
Provide dolls with a range of skin tones, and real-scale kit — nappies, bottles, a bath with real water, clothes with manageable poppers.
Sing the setting's lullabies at doll bedtime so children have a soothing repertoire of their own.
Ask about children's real babyhoods and their families' baby routines — bring in photos of them as babies if families are happy to share.
When a new sibling arrives at home, quietly stock up: this play is where the big feelings land, so give it time and stay close.
key_questions: Why do you think your baby is crying — what might she need?
What did you eat and do when you were a baby?
How do we hold a baby so she feels safe?
Who looks after the babies in your family?
What helps your baby settle when nothing seems to work?

impact.text: Younger children feed, rock and pat their babies in brief tender episodes with real-looking props.
Older children sustain whole days of family life for their babies — feeds, walks, bathtime, bedtime — with shared roles and storylines.
Children narrate the baby's day aloud as they play — 'she's tired now, we're going home, shh'.
Children name the baby's feelings — hungry, sad, tired, cross — and choose comfort that fits, showing real empathy along the way.
Children copy the kindness modelled around them — fetching blankets, patting backs, whispering near the sleeping baby.
Children spoon-feed, bathe, dress and fasten with careful hands — poppers, straps, tiny sleeves and all.
Children compare then and now — 'when I was a baby I had a bottle, now I use a cup' — and talk about who cared for them.
Children talk about how their own family looks after babies and notice that friends' families do it differently — and that's interesting.

enhancements: Dolls with a genuine range of skin tones, plus twins for sharing crises.
A real baby bath with warm water, flannels and towels for proper bathtime.
Real nappies, wipes and a changing mat at a child-height changing station.
Slings and wraps so babies can be carried the ways families really carry them.
A pram, a cot and a bedtime basket — storybook, lullaby cards, tiny blanket.
Photos of the children themselves as babies, shared by families, displayed by the cots.
Weaning kitchen provocation: bibs, small bowls, spoons and playdough 'baby food'.

playing_exploring: Children replay the most familiar experience they have — being cared for — from the caring side.
Bathing, dressing and feeding invite full sensory involvement: real water, real fastenings, real tenderness.
active_learning: A crying baby is a problem that won't wait — children keep trying feed, wind, rock, sing until something works.
creating_thinking: Children invent what their baby needs, feels and does next, holding the whole little life in their heads.
